background:
2 John: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes

Study notes · dates are approximate and scholars vary

At a glance

2 John is a short note, small enough to fit on a single sheet of papyrus, from “the elder” to “the elect lady and her children.” It urges a church to keep walking in truth and love and not to welcome traveling teachers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. It dates from about AD 90–95.

QuestionTraditional viewNotes
Author“The elder” (v. 1)Traditionally John the apostle, writing near the end of his life.
DateAbout AD 90–95Probably close in time to 1 and 3 John.
Recipients“The elect lady and her children”Most likely a local church and its members, with a “sister” church sending greetings (v. 13); possibly a particular woman and her family.
Length13 versesAbout 245 words in Greek, typical of a private letter on one papyrus sheet.
The danger“Many deceivers” who deny “that Jesus Christ cometh in the flesh” (v. 7)The same false teaching addressed in 1 John.
The instructionDo not receive such teachers into your house (v. 10)Hospitality, essential for traveling ministers, could also spread error.

2 John holds truth and love together: love means walking in God's commandments, and truth means remaining in the teaching of Christ.

The time map

The shaded band marks the likely date of John's letters, late in Domitian's reign, when John was the last living apostle.

Ephesus under Domitian

John's letters were written to churches around Ephesus in the 90s, when the faith was about sixty years old.

  • Domitian (AD 81–96). An autocratic emperor who liked to be addressed as “lord and god.” Christian tradition remembers persecution late in his reign.
  • The emperor cult. Around AD 89–90 Ephesus dedicated a great temple to the Flavian emperors, with a colossal statue. Honoring the emperor was a civic duty.
  • Idols everywhere. Ephesus was the city of Artemis, magic and many gods. John's last words are, “Guard yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:21).
  • Greek ideas about the body. Popular philosophy often saw the spirit as good and the body as worthless. Some taught that Christ only seemed to have a real body (an idea later called Docetism).
  • Cerinthus. A teacher in Asia who said the divine Christ came on the man Jesus at His baptism and left before the cross. Irenaeus tells that John once fled a bathhouse in Ephesus when he saw Cerinthus there.
  • Traveling teachers. Christian missionaries moved between churches and depended on hospitality, which false teachers could exploit (2 John 10; 3 John 5–8).

Against these ideas, John insists that “Jesus Christ is come in the flesh” (1 John 4:2) and that real fellowship with God shows itself in love and obedience.

The churches around Ephesus

By John's day there were churches across the province of Asia, many of them named in Revelation 2–3.

  • Ephesus. Capital of Asia, home to a church for over forty years, founded through Paul and led later by John.
  • A split. Some members had left the church, denying that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh (1 John 2:19, 22; 4:2–3).
  • House churches. Believers met in homes; “the elect lady and her children” (2 John 1) may be a church and its members.
  • Gaius and Diotrephes. 3 John shows one church leader, Diotrephes, refusing John's messengers, while Gaius welcomed them.
  • “The elder.” John calls himself simply “the elder” (2 John 1; 3 John 1), the aged leader known to all the churches.
  • Patmos. A small island about 60 miles offshore, where John was exiled and saw the visions of Revelation (Rev 1:9).

Maps: then and now

Ephesus was the hub of a network of cities in the province of Asia, linked by Roman roads, the same churches later addressed in Revelation.

Today Ephesus lies near Selçuk in Türkiye, where the ruins of a great Basilica of St. John stand over his traditional tomb.

Around the world in the AD 90s

John's letters were written as Rome reached the height of its power.

RegionWhat was happening
RomeDomitian rebuilt the city and its palaces; he was assassinated in AD 96, and the elderly Nerva and then Trajan followed.
BritainRoman forts stretched into Scotland after Agricola's campaigns (AD 77–84).
Germany and the DanubeDomitian fought the Chatti and the Dacians and fortified the frontier.
JudeaJerusalem lay in ruins with a Roman legion camped there; Jewish life reorganized around rabbis at Yavneh.
ChinaUnder the Eastern Han, the general Ban Chao controlled the Silk Road; in AD 97 his envoy Gan Ying set out to reach Rome.
IndiaThe Kushan Empire ruled from Central Asia into northern India.
The AmericasTeotihuacan was one of the world's largest cities; the Maya were building early cities in the lowlands.

How the setting shapes the study

2 John's brief instructions make sense in the world of traveling teachers and house churches.

PassageConnection to the times
2 John 1“The elect lady” may be a personified church, as “thine elect sister” (v. 13) may be another church.
2 John 7Teachers denied Christ's real humanity, like Cerinthus in Asia.
2 John 10Churches met in homes, so receiving a teacher “into your house” meant giving him a platform.
2 John 12“Paper and ink”: papyrus sheets and ink made of soot and gum.

John would rather talk “face to face” (v. 12), but this short letter guards the church until he can come.

items.text: The elder unto the elect lady and her children, whom I love in truth; and not I only, but also all they that know the truth;
for the truth’s sake which abideth in us, and it shall be with us for ever:
Grace, mercy, peace shall be with us, from God the Father, and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, in truth and love.
Walk in Truth and Love vv. 4–6
I rejoice greatly that I have found certain of thy children walking in truth, even as we received commandment from the Father.
And now I beseech thee, lady, not as though I wrote to thee a new commandment, but that which we had from the beginning, that we love one another.
And this is love, that we should walk after his commandments. This is the commandment, even as ye heard from the beginning, that ye should walk in it.
For many deceivers are gone forth into the world, even they that confess not that Jesus Christ cometh in the flesh. This is the deceiver and the antichrist.
Look to yourselves, that ye lose not the things which we have wrought, but that ye receive a full reward.
Whosoever goeth onward and abideth not in the teaching of Christ, hath not God: he that abideth in the teaching, the same hath both the Father and the Son.
If any one cometh unto you, and bringeth not this teaching, receive him not into your house, and give him no greeting:
for he that giveth him greeting partaketh in his evil works.
Having many things to write unto you, I would not write them with paper and ink: but I hope to come unto you, and to speak face to face, that your joy may be made full.
The children of thine elect sister salute thee.

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: What does the elder say about walking in truth and love in vv. 4–6, and what warning does he give in vv. 7–11?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: Since traveling teachers depended on hospitality in house churches, why was the elder's instruction about whom to receive (vv. 10–11) so practically important?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: How do you balance warm hospitality with care about which teaching you help spread, and what would that look like in your home or group?

wrap.title: 2 John In Summary
paras: 2 John is a brief letter from “the elder” to “the elect lady and her children,” probably a local church and its members. John rejoices to have found some of them walking in the truth, as the Father commanded, and he reminds them of the commandment they had from the beginning: that they love one another. Love, he explains, means walking according to God's commandments.

Then comes a warning. Many deceivers have gone out into the world who do not confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh; such a person is the deceiver and the antichrist. The church must watch itself so as not to lose what it has worked for, but receive a full reward. Anyone who goes beyond the teaching of Christ does not have God, while whoever remains in it has both the Father and the Son.

John gives a practical instruction: if a traveling teacher comes bringing a different message, the church should not receive him into the house or give him a greeting, for that would be sharing in his evil works. In a world where Christian teachers depended on hospitality and churches met in homes, welcoming someone meant endorsing and supporting his ministry.

John closes by saying he has much more to write but hopes to come and speak face to face, so that their joy may be full, and he sends greetings from the children of their “elect sister.” The message in one line: love and truth belong together, so believers should love one another by keeping God's commands and guard their fellowship against teaching that denies who Jesus truly is.
